'''Alden Stephen Rochè Jr.''' ({{IPAc-en|r|oʊ|ˈ|ʃ|eɪ}} {{respell|roh|SHAY}};<ref>[https://media.denverbroncos.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/1970.pdf Denver Broncos 1970 Press-Radio-Television Guide (pronunciations on page 43).] Retrieved November 2, 2020</ref> April 9, 1945 – May 29, 2022) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played for the [[Denver Broncos]], [[Green Bay Packers]], and [[Seattle Seahawks]] from 1970 to 1978, having earlier played [[college football]] at [[Southern University]].

==Early life==
Roche was born in [[New Orleans]] on April 9, 1945.<ref name="PFR player">{{cite web|title=Alden Roche Stats|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RochAl20.htm|access-date=June 3, 2022|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC}}</ref><ref name="statscrew.com 2021">{{cite web | title=Alden Roche football Statistics on StatsCrew.com | website=statscrew.com | date=March 6, 2021 | url=https://www.statscrew.com/football/stats/p-rocheald001 | access-date=June 3, 2022}}</ref>  He attended [[Xavier University Preparatory School]] in his hometown.<ref name="PFR player"/><ref name="Pro Football Archives 1945">{{cite web | title=Alden Roche NFL Stats | website=Pro Football Archives | date=April 9, 1945 | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerr/roch00200.html | access-date=June 3, 2022}}</ref>  He then studied at [[Southern University]], where he played [[college football]] for the [[Southern Jaguars and Lady Jaguars|Southern Jaguars]].<ref name="PFR player"/>  He received first-team All-American honors and was selected as an All-[[Southwestern Athletic Conference|SWAC]] defensive end.  He was also named the university's most valuable defensive lineman in 1969.<ref name="GNOHOF">{{cite web|title=Alden Roche|url=https://allstatesugarbowl.org/sports/2022/4/26/alden-roche.aspx|access-date=June 3, 2022|publisher=[[Sugar Bowl]]|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220603062742/https://allstatesugarbowl.org/sports/2022/4/26/alden-roche.aspx|archivedate=June 3, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>  Roche was drafted by the [[Denver Broncos]] in the second round (37th overall selection) of the [[1970 NFL draft]].<ref name="PFR player"/>

==Career==
Roche made his NFL debut with the Broncos on September 20, 1970, at the age of 25, in a 25–10 win over the [[Buffalo Bills]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RochAl20/gamelog/1970/|title=Alden Roche 1970 Game Log|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=June 3, 2022}}</ref>  He played in all 14 games during his rookie season,<ref name="PFR player"/> before being traded to the [[Green Bay Packers]] for [[Don Horn]] on January 28 the following year.  The transaction also included a swap of [[1971 NFL draft|1971]] first-round picks, with the Packers selecting [[John Brockington]] at 9th and the Broncos choosing [[Marv Montgomery]] at 12th.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1971/01/29/archives/patriots-choose-plunkett-as-no-1-in-college-draft-spurning-trade.html Wallace, William N. "Patriots Choose Plunkett as No. 1 in College Draft, Spurning Trade Offers," ''The New York Times'', Friday, January 29, 1971.] Retrieved November 2, 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.prosportstransactions.com/football/DraftTrades/Years/1971.htm 1971 NFL Draft Pick Transactions, January 28 (Rounds 1–7) & 29 (Rounds 8–17) – Pro Sports Transactions.] Retrieved November 2, 2020</ref>

The Packers appointed [[Dan Devine]] as head coach six games into the [[1971 NFL season|1971 season]].<ref name="Aldridge bio">{{cite web|title=Lionel Aldridge|url=https://www.packers.com/history/hof/lionel-aldridge|first=Cliff|last=Christl|access-date=June 3, 2022|publisher=Green Bay Packers}}</ref>  He chose Roche as the starting right [[defensive end]], replacing the incumbent [[Lionel Aldridge]], a holdover from the Packers' glory days under [[Vince Lombardi]].<ref name="Aldridge bio"/><ref name="Packers obit">{{cite news|title=Former Packers defensive lineman Alden Roche dies at 77|url=https://www.packers.com/news/former-packers-defensive-lineman-alden-roche-dies-at-77|first=Cliff|last=Christl|date=June 2, 2022|access-date=June 3, 2022|publisher=Green Bay Packers|archive-date=June 5, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220605164023/https://www.packers.com/news/former-packers-defensive-lineman-alden-roche-dies-at-77|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Roche was noted for his versatility – filling in for [[Mike McCoy (defensive tackle)|Mike McCoy]] at left [[defensive tackle]] and [[Clarence Williams (defensive end)|Clarence Williams]] at left defensive end<ref name=Christl3>{{cite news|title=The best of the gory years' grunts|url=https://www.packers.com/news/the-best-of-the-gory-years-grunts|first=Cliff|last=Christl|date=October 1, 2020|access-date=June 3, 2022|publisher=Green Bay Packers|archive-date=June 3, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220603121604/https://www.packers.com/news/the-best-of-the-gory-years-grunts|url-status=dead}}</ref> – and won the Packers [[most valuable player]] award for defense that year.<ref name=Christl3/><ref>{{cite book| title=The Best Wisconsin Sports Arguments: The 100 Most Controversial, Debatable Questions for Die-Hard Fans| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_baYavYAPgIC&pg=PA97| publisher=Sourcebooks, Inc.| date=September 1, 2009| last=Kendeigh| first=Andy| page=97| isbn=9781402247347}}</ref>  He went on to hold the starting role for the next five seasons, playing in all but one game during his tenure with the franchise.<ref name="Packers obit"/><ref name=Christl3/>  He played an integral role in helping the Packers finish second in the league in team defense during the [[1972 NFL season|1972 season]], when the team won what was ultimately their only division title between 1967 and 1995.<ref name="Packers obit"/><ref name=Christl3/>  He also tied with McCoy for the franchise lead in [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] (8.5) in 1976.<ref name="Packers obit"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Mike P. McCoy helped Packers in a big way|url=https://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/mike-p-mccoy-helped-packers-in-a-big-way-b99565911z1-324005711.html|first=Martin|last=Hendricks|date=September 2, 2015|access-date=June 3, 2022|newspaper=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel}}</ref>  Roche formed a noted defensive partnership with Williams.<ref name=Zagorski>{{cite book|title=The Year the Packers Came Back: Green Bay's 1972 Resurgence|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ON6_DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA202|publisher=McFarland|date=November 20, 2019|last=Zagorski|first=Joe|pages=202–203|isbn=9781476674247}}</ref>

Roche joined the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in 1977.  He spent his last two years in the NFL with the franchise before retiring after the [[1978 NFL season|1978 season]].<ref name="PFR player"/><ref name=Zagorski/>

==Personal life==
Roche was inducted into the Greater New Orleans Sports Hall of Fame in 1991.<ref name="GNOHOF"/>  His grandson, Jay'Shawn Washington, played college football for the [[Southern Miss Golden Eagles football|Southern Miss Golden Eagles]] from 2015 to 2018.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jay'Shawn Washington – Football|url=https://southernmiss.com/sports/football/roster/jay-shawn-washington/3868|access-date=June 3, 2022|publisher=Southern Miss Golden Eagles|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220603063417/https://southernmiss.com/sports/football/roster/jay-shawn-washington/3868|archivedate=June 3, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>

Roche died on May 29, 2022, in [[Marrero, Louisiana]], at the age of 77.<ref name="Packers obit"/><ref>[https://obits.nola.com/us/obituaries/nola/name/alden-roche-obituary?id=35094194 Alden Stephen Roche' Jr.]</ref>

'''Albert Timothy Bentley''' (born August 15, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). Bentley began his professional career in the USFL with the [[Michigan Panthers]] and [[Oakland Invaders]] from 1984 to 1985. After the USFL folded, he played for the NFL's [[Indianapolis Colts]] and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] from 1985 to 1992. Bentley played [[college football]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]].

==Early life==
Albert Bentley was born on August 15, 1960, in [[Immokalee, Florida]] one of twelve children. He attended [[Immokalee High School]] where he was a tailback on the football team and a member of the [[wrestling]] and [[track and field]] teams. In his senior year, he was named Most Valuable Player on all three teams.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rife |first1=Tom |title=Immokalee Pays Tribute To Athletes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/798758031/?match=1&clipping_id=146909824 |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The Naples Daily News |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=May 25, 1979}}</ref>

On the football team, Immokalee only won two games during Bentley's senior year. However, Bentley rushed for nearly 1,000 yards.<ref name="mystery">{{cite news |last1=Archdeacon |first1=Tom |title=Albert Bentley: U-M's mystery man beat the odds |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-miami-news-albert-bentley-u-ms-mys/146910586/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The Miami News |date=October 31, 1979}}</ref> He only received one football scholarship offer from [[Findlay Oilers|Findlay University]] in Ohio. He declined that offer and chose to attend the University of Miami without a scholarship after speaking with then-head coach [[Lou Saban]]. Saban encouraged Bentley to try out and with the possibly of earning a scholarship.<ref name="odds">{{cite news |last1=Wojciechowski |first1=Gene |title=Bentley beat odds to earn UM scholarship |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/south-florida-sun-sentinel-bentley-beat/146851258/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=South Florida Sun Sentinel |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=September 15, 1982}}</ref>

==College career==
Prior to Bentley's arrival, Saban left Miami following the 1978 season and was replaced by head coach [[Howard Schnellenberger]]. Bentley was a freshman walk-on at Miami in 1979, and saw limited playing time.<ref>{{cite news |title=College Football |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/628236775/?match=1&clipping_id=146910357 |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The Miami Herald |date=October 26, 1979}}</ref> In a Miami junior varsity game against [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State]], Bentley nearly returned a kickoff for a touchdown before a Florida State player came off the sidelines to tackle him near the end zone. The referees did not see the infraction, but the Miami coaching staff took notice of his playing ability.<ref name=mystery /> He saw varsity action as a kick returner throughout the rest of the season.

Bentley quit the football team during the 1980–81 season, opting to focus on his studies.<ref name=odds /> He returned for the 1981 season, and again saw limited action as a non-scholarship player. He recorded 10 rushing attempts for 53 yards and nearly scored before fumbling the ball at the goal line. Most of Bentley's playing time came on kickoff and punt coverage.<ref name="cfb">{{cite web |title=Albert Bentley |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/albert-bentley-1.html |website=Sports Reference CFB |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

In the spring of 1982, Schnellenberger offered Bentley a scholarship for his junior season. He shared [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] duties with [[Speedy Neal]] and recorded 64 carries for 247 yards and one touchdown.<ref name =cfb />

In his senior season, Bentley became the Hurricanes' leading rusher with 144 attempts for 722 yards and five touchdowns. He also caught 32 passes for 294 yards and one touchdown. With quarterback [[Bernie Kosar]] and Bentley leading the team, the Hurricanes went 10–1 on the regular season finishing ranked #5 in the [[AP poll]]. They earned a place in the [[1984 Orange Bowl]] against then-undefeated and #1-ranked [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska]]. In the third quarter, Bentley rushed for what became the winning touchdown of the Orange Bowl. Miami led 31–17 at the end of the third quarter, but Nebraska scored two touchdowns in the fourth quarter and opted for a two-point conversion on the final touchdown, which failed. Miami won 31–30 and were named [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|consensus national champions]] with an 11–1 record.<ref name="hof">{{cite web|url=http://umsportshalloffame.com/inductees.asp?ID=7 |title=Albert Bentley |publisher=University of Miami Sports Hall of Fame Inductee |access-date=August 24, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101020011606/http://umsportshalloffame.com/inductees.asp?ID=7 |archive-date=October 20, 2010}}</ref>

Bentley was inducted into the University of Miami Sports Hall of Fame in 2007.<ref name=hof />

==Professional career==
In January 1984, Bentley was selected by the [[Chicago Blitz]] with the seventh overall selection in the [[1984 USFL draft|1984 USFL draft]].<ref>{{cite news |title=USFL |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/simi-valley-star-usfl/146913566/ |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=Simi Valley Star |agency=UPI |date=January 4, 1984}}</ref> However, Bentley's contract negotiations with the Blitz stalled following the draft. As the 1984 USFL season got underway, the Blitz traded him to the [[Michigan Panthers]] who were looking to replace running back [[Ken Lacy]] after he moved to the NFL.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brennan |first1=Christine |title=Bentley considers Panther's contract |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-miami-herald-bentley-considers-panth/146914563/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |work=The Miami Herald |date=April 17, 1984}}</ref> Bentley signed with the Panthers and began his professional career in the USFL.

Bentley was later selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the second round (36th overall) of the [[1984 NFL Supplemental Draft of USFL and CFL Players|1984 NFL Supplemental Draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

===Michigan Panthers/Oakland Invaders (1984–1985)===
Bentley signed with the Michigan Panthers on April 17, 1984, following week eight of the USFL season. Bentley was used mostly as a backup running back while also returning kickoffs for the remaining 10 games of the season. Bentley recorded 18 carries for 60 yards and returned 19 kickoffs for 425 yards on the year.<ref name="usfl">{{cite web |title=Albert Bentley USFL Statistics |url=https://www.usflsite.com/players/Albert_Bentley/p-bentlalb001 |website=USFL Site |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref> The Panthers went 12–6 in the regular season and lost to the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]] in the Divisional Round of the playoffs.

In 1985, the Panthers organization merged with the [[Oakland Invaders]] and continued playing under the Invaders name. Bentley stayed with Oakland, where he led the team with 191 rushes for 1,020 yards and four touchdowns, while adding 44 catches for 441 yards and three touchdowns.<ref name=usfl /> The Invaders went 13–4–1 on the regular season and defeated the [[Tampa Bay Bandits]] and [[Memphis Showboats]] in the playoffs to earn a spot in the 1985 USFL Championship Game. The Invaders lost 24–28 to the [[Baltimore Stars]] in what became the USFL's final game.

===Indianapolis Colts (1985–1991)===
Following the demise of the USFL, Bentley signed a contract with the Indianapolis Colts on September 3, 1985. The Colts had selected Bentley in the 1984 NFL Supplemental Draft and retained his NFL playing rights.<ref>{{cite news |title=Ex-USFL Star reaches agreement with Colts |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star-ex-usfl-star-reach/146917554/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |work=The Indianapolis Star |date=September 4, 1985}}</ref>

In his first year with the Colts, Bentley appeared in 15 games with 54 rushes for 288 yards and two touchdowns while returning 27 kickoffs for 674 yards and a career-high 25.0-yard average return.<ref name="pfr">{{cite web |title=Albert Bentley |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BentAl00.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref> In week five against the [[Buffalo Bills]], Bentley recorded his first 100-yard rushing performance in the NFL with 17 carries for 100 yards.<ref>{{cite web |title=Buffalo Bills at Indianapolis Colts - October 6th, 1985 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198510060clt.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref> Bentley scored one rushing touchdown each in the final two weeks of the season against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and [[Houston Oilers]], respectively. The Colts went 4–11 on the season.<ref>{{cite web |title=1985 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1985.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

In 1986, Bentley continued to serve as a backup to [[Randy McMillan]], splitting time throughout the season with [[George Wonsley]] while also returning kickoffs. He recorded 73 carries for 351 yards and three touchdowns with 25 receptions for 230 yards. Bentley had 32 kick returns for 687 yards, averaging 21.5 yards per return.<ref name=pfr /> Bentley missed four games after being placed on [[injured reserve]] with a calf muscle injury, but still managed to be the Colts' second-leading rusher on the season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Transactions |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-news-transactions/146983401/ |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The Indianapolis News |date=October 21, 1986}}</ref> The Colts started the 1986 season at 0–13, firing head coach [[Rod Dowhower]] and replacing him with [[Ron Meyer]]. Meyer won the final three games, ending the Colts' season at 3–13.<ref>{{cite web |title=1986 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1986.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

In 1987, Bentley had his best statistical season in the NFL. However, a new Colts running back and the [[1987 NFL season#The NFLPA strike|1987 player's strike]] stood in his way. The NFL canceled all week three games and used replacement players for weeks four through six. At the conclusion of the strike, the Colts traded for running back [[Eric Dickerson]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Albert Bentley realizes $5 million players play over those... |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/11/01/Albert-Bentley-realizes-5-million-players-play-over-those/5720562741200/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=UPI |date=November 1, 1987}}</ref> Bentley was Dickerson's backup for the remainder of the season, but still produced in the 12 games he appeared with 142 rushes for 631 yards and a career-high seven rushing touchdowns. He added 34 receptions for 447 yards and two touchdowns while also returning 22 kicks for 500 yards.<ref name=pfr /> The Colts won the [[AFC East]] Division at 9–6 and earned their first playoff appearance since moving to Indianapolis. They lost in the [[1987-88 NFL playoffs]] Divisional Round 21–38 to the [[Cleveland Browns]].<ref>{{cite web |title=1987 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1987.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

By 1988, Dickerson was taking the majority of the snaps at running back leaving Bentley to start only two games. Dickerson led the league in rushing, and Bentley found a complimentary role in the Colts' offense. He appeared in all 16 games with 45 carries for 230 yards and two touchdowns and added 26 receptions for 252 yards and one touchdown. As a kick returner, Bentley saw his largest career workload with 39 returns for 775 yards.<ref name =pfr /> The Colts finished with a 9–7 record, but missed the playoffs.<ref>{{cite web |title=1988 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1988.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

For the 1989 season, the Colts moved to a two-running back formation and Bentley saw an uptick in his playing time. He finished the season with 75 rushing attempts for 299 yards and one touchdown and had 52 receptions for 525 yards and three touchdowns. Bentley joined wide receivers [[Andre Rison]] and [[Bill Brooks (wide receiver)|Bill Brooks]] as the first trio in Colts history to record 500 receiving yards each in one season.<ref name="flashback">{{cite web |title=Colts.com Flashback: Albert Bentley |url=https://www.colts.com/news/colts-com-flashback-albert-bentley-7437133 |website=Colts.com |publisher=Indianapolis Colts |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref> The Colts finished the season at 8-8.

In 1990, Bentley was again productive on the ground and had his best season as a pass catcher. He posted 137 carries for 556 yards and four touchdowns and added career-highs with a team-leading 71 receptions for 664 yards and two touchdowns. For the second consecutive season, Bentley was part of a trio of Colts receivers with over 500 yards, the others being Brooks and [[Jessie Hester]]. The Colts finished the season at 7–9.<ref>{{cite web |title=1990 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1990.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

In 1991, Bentley injured his shoulder in a preseason game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]]. He missed week one, and upon his return in week two he suffered a knee injury against the [[Miami Dolphins]]. Bentley was placed on injured reserve and missed the rest of the 1991 season.<ref name=flashback />

Bentley was prepared to take over the Colts starting role with the departure of Dickerson after the 1991 season. Bentley appeared in all four of the Colts 1992 preseason games, but with lingering doubts about his knee he was released on August 31, 1992.<ref>{{cite news |title=Colts cut veteran Bentley |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-news-colts-cut-veteran/147009675/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The Indianapolis News |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=August 31, 1992}}</ref>

===Pittsburgh Steelers (1992)===
Bentley signed with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] on September 16, 1992.<ref>{{cite news |title=Steelers ink Albert Bentley |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/intelligencer-journal-steelers-ink-alber/147010120/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=Intelligencer Journal |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |agency=Associated Press |date=September 17, 1992}}</ref> Bentley returned one kickoff for 17 yards in two appearances with the Steelers before being released on November 16, 1992.<ref name=pfr /><ref>{{cite news |title=Transactions |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-york-dispatch-transactions/147010456/ |access-date=May 9, 2024 |work=The York Dispatch |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=November 17, 1992}}</ref>

'''Alan Stuart Veingrad''' (born July 24, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[East Texas A&M Lions football|East Texas A&M Lions]]. Veingrad played in the NFL for the [[Green Bay Packers]] for five seasons, and for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] for two season, winning [[Super Bowl XXVII]] with the team over the [[Buffalo Bills]]. In his career he played a total of 86 games.

==Early and personal life==
Veingrad was born in Brooklyn, New York, lived in [[Englishtown, New Jersey]], from ages three to nine, before moving to Miami, Florida, in 1972.<ref name=autogenerated4>[http://www.aish.com/sp/so/48916972.html Life after the Super Bowl<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref name=autogenerated2>[https://azjewishpost.com/2018/community-sets-jewish-football-pro-on-spiritual-journey/ "‘Community’ sets Jewish football pro on spiritual journey" | ''AZ Jewish Post''<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He is Jewish, attended [[Hebrew school]] and was [[bar mitzvah]], and grew up in a Jewish household.<ref name=autogenerated4 /><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=QNaczbX4f78C&dq=%22Alan+Veingrad%22&pg=PA136 ''The 100 Greatest Jews in Sports: Ranked According to Achievement'' - B. P. Robert Stephen Silverman<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=dDyEVDIA3aIC&dq=%22Alan+Veingrad%22&pg=PA26 ''The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heroes: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports ...'' - Peter S. Horvitz<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref name=autogenerated1>[https://books.google.com/books?id=dAq4TGQsWwwC&dq=%22Alan+Veingrad%22&pg=PA206 ''Day by Day in Jewish Sports History'' - Bob Wechsler<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

He attended [[Miami Sunset High School]]. There, he competed in [[American football|football]] and was captain of his high school team as well as All-Conference and All-American, and in [[track and field]] in [[discus]] and  [[shot put]].<ref name=autogenerated2 />

He married in 1993.<ref name=autogenerated4 /> Veingrad lived in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida]], and lives in [[Boca Raton, Florida]], where he works for [[AIPAC]] to advocate for Israel.<ref name=autogenerated4 /><ref>Horn, Barry. [http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/dn/latestnews/stories/092307dnspo1aveingrad.3acaa69.html "Ex-Cowboy Finds Faith After Football."], ''[[Dallas Morning News]]'', September 23, 2007.</ref><ref>Dallas Morning News  about Alan Veingrad http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/spe/2007/shlomo/</ref><ref name=autogenerated3>[https://www.crescentcityjewishnews.com/alan-veingrad-the-journey-to-shlomo/ "Alan Veingrad: the journey to Shlomo" - ''Crescent City Jewish News''<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==College career==
Veingrad received a scholarship from East Texas State University (now [[East Texas A&M University]]), in [[Commerce, Texas]], to play [[college football]] and throw the [[discus]].<ref name=autogenerated4 /><ref name=autogenerated2 /><ref name=autogenerated1 /><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=Lr1tAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Alan+Veingrad%22 ''Jewish Currents''<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He was converted to an [[offensive lineman]] in football, and in 1984 he was named [[Lone Star Conference|Lone Star]] All-Conference, Lone Star Offensive Lineman of the Year and received [[NCAA Division II|Division II]] and National Strength & Conditioning [[All-America]]n honors.<ref name=autogenerated3 /><ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2206&dat=19850814&id=8qImAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ywEGAAAAIBAJ&pg=4980,3753949 x]{{Dead link|date=August 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> The six-foot, five-inch Veingrad worked out extensively and ate a high-carbohydrate diet, resulting in by the end of his freshman year weighing 220 pounds, and by the end of his college career weighing 270 pounds.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> He ultimately earned his degree.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> He was inducted into the school's Athletic Hall of Fame in October 2006.<ref>[http://lionathletics.cstv.com/hallfame/tame-hallfame.html Texas A&M University–Commerce / East Texas State University – Athletic hall of Fame Members] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207020217/http://lionathletics.cstv.com/hallfame/tame-hallfame.html |date=2019-02-07 }}, ''[[CSTV]]''. Retrieved October 31, 2007.</ref>

==Professional career==
Veingrad was considered small for his position, and wasn't selected in the [[1985 NFL draft]].<ref name=autogenerated3 /> Although he was selected by the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]] in the eleventh round (163rd overall) of the [[1985 USFL draft]], he opted to sign as an [[undrafted free agent]] with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. He was cut after 10 days.<ref name=autogenerated3 />

The [[Houston Oilers]] claimed him off [[waiver]]s, but eventually released him before the start of the [[1985 NFL season|1985 season]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1368&dat=19870530&id=sIZRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=qRIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4771,8157699 |title=''The Milwaukee Sentinel''<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2015-06-16 |archive-date=2016-04-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160415200628/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1368&dat=19870530&id=sIZRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=qRIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4771,8157699 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=autogenerated3 />

In [[1986 NFL season|1986]] he signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]] as a [[free agent]], and became the opening day starter at right [[offensive tackle]].<ref name="nyt">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/06/us/06religion.html|title=A Rare Blend, Pro Football and Hasidic Judaism |last=Freedman|first=Samuel G.|date=February 5, 2010|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 29, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207052245/http://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/06/us/06religion.html |archive-date=February 7, 2010}}</ref> He sat out all of the [[1988 NFL season|1988]] season with a career-threatening hip injury.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> His return and consistent play kept heralded rookie [[Tony Mandarich]] on the bench in [[1989 NFL season|1989]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1368&dat=19891011&id=cHtQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=tRIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6248,2806010 |title=''The Milwaukee Sentinel''<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2015-06-16 |archive-date=2016-04-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160406234026/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1368&dat=19891011&id=cHtQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=tRIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6248,2806010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In [[1991 NFL season|1991]], after four seasons as a starter for the Packers, he signed in [[Plan B free agency]] with the [[Dallas Cowboys]], where as a backup at [[Offensive tackle|tackle]] and [[guard (American football)|guard]], he helped [[Emmitt Smith]] win the [[NFL]] rushing title in [[1991 NFL season|1991]] and [[1992 NFL season|1992]].<ref name=autogenerated3 /> He also helped the Cowboys reach [[Super Bowl XXVII]], although he was one of two players declared inactive for [[Super Bowl]] Sunday (the other was [[Robert Williams (cornerback)|Robert Williams]]).

In his NFL career, he played in 86 games.<ref name=autogenerated2 />

==Retirement and public speaker==

Following the [[Super Bowl XXVII]] win, Veingrad retired from football in 1993  and returned to Florida.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> Veingrad speaks professionally to corporations about leadership and professional development.<ref name=autogenerated3 />

==National Jewish Sports Hall of Fame==
Veingrad was inducted into the [[National Jewish Sports Hall of Fame]] on April 19, 2010.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> The ceremony was held at the Suffolk Y Jewish Community Center in [[Commack, New York]]. The organization chronicles and celebrates Jewish involvement in sports, and includes Jewish sports legends such as [[Sandy Koufax]], [[Red Auerbach]], [[Kerri Strug]], and [[Hank Greenberg]].<ref>Decotis, Mark. [http://www.floridatoday.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=2009909250337 "Veingrad to Speak Locally"]{{dead link|date=March 2010}}, ''[[Florida Today]]'', September 25, 2009</ref><ref name=autogenerated3 />

'''Albert Ray Lewis''' (born October 6, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and the [[Oakland Raiders|Los Angeles/Oakland Raiders]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Grambling State Tigers football|Grambling State Tigers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Albert Lewis Biography |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/bio/_/id/6555/albert-lewis |access-date=2024-12-12 |website=ESPN |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
Lewis was a third-round draft pick (61st overall) by the Chiefs in the [[1983 NFL draft]]. His career spanned 16 seasons in which he recorded 42 interceptions, 12.5 sacks, 13 forced fumbles, 13 fumbles recoveries and 2 touchdowns. In addition to his play on defense, Lewis blocked 11 kicks in 11 seasons with the Chiefs.

Lewis was named the Chiefs MVP for the 1986 season after he recorded 69 tackles (61 solo), four interceptions, two fumble recoveries, one sack and one blocked punt. During his time in Kansas City, the Chiefs made the playoffs five times.  This included an appearance in the [[1993-94 NFL playoffs|1993 AFC Championship game]]. Lewis finished with 38 interceptions in 11 seasons with the Chiefs, the fifth-highest total in franchise history. Twenty of those came in his first four seasons before opposing teams decided not to throw to his side of the field as much.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/team/chiefs-history/hall-of-fame/albert-lewis.html |title=KCChiefs.com |access-date=August 19, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611232025/http://www.kcchiefs.com/team/chiefs-history/hall-of-fame/albert-lewis.html |archive-date=June 11, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He played in 150 games for the Chiefs and was a starter in 128 of them.<ref>[http://www.arrowheadpride.com/2009/8/4/976584/the-greatest-kansas-city-chiefs-by arrowheadpride.com]</ref> Lewis spent the final five seasons of his career with the Raiders. While with the team, he became the oldest player to score a defensive touchdown (38 years, 26 days) on November 1, 1998, when he returned an interception 74 yards for a touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks, his first and only interception return for a touchdown in his career.

Lewis retired from the NFL after the 1998 season.

Lewis was known for his excellent acceleration and speed, at one point running a 4.38 in the 40-yard dash.<ref name="sichip">{{cite magazine |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1140078/1/index.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103000418/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1140078/1/index.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 3, 2012|title= A Chip Off the Old Block|magazine=Sports Illustrated |access-date=August 18, 2010 | first=Jill | last=Lieber|date=December 2, 1991}}</ref> At 6' 2", he was one of the tallest cornerbacks in the NFL at the time. He also had 35-inch long arms and a 38-inch vertical leap.<ref name="sichip"/> Lewis credited his strong determination and work-ethic to his father, Brad.<ref name="sichip"/><ref>[https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-12-23-sp-12214-story.html latimes.com]</ref>

==Legacy==
Lewis was named to the Chiefs 25-Year All-Time Team in 1987 and was inducted into the [[Kansas City Chiefs|Chiefs]] Hall of Fame on March 4, 2007.

In 1999, Lewis bought ''Greystone'', a {{convert|320|acre|ha|abbr=on}} horse ranch north in [[Centreville, Mississippi]].<ref>{{cite web | last = McCraine | first = Don | title = Former NFL Cornerback Albert Lewis Finds New Challenge at Centreville Ranch | publisher = Associated Press | url = http://www.majorwager.com/forums/mess-hall/122201-former-nfl-cornerback-albert-lewis-finds-new-challenge-centreville-ranch.html | access-date = March 16, 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140316182252/http://www.majorwager.com/forums/mess-hall/122201-former-nfl-cornerback-albert-lewis-finds-new-challenge-centreville-ranch.html | archive-date = March 16, 2014 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

In July 2008, Lewis, along with former Chiefs teammate [[Kevin Ross (American football)|Kevin Ross]], was named to the [[NFL Network]]'s "Top 10 Cornerback Tandems" list.<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d807a1f2b&template=with-video&confirm=true nfl.com]</ref> He was named as a finalist for the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] for the first time in 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=Thomas, Revis, Freeney among '23 HOF finalists |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/35380691/pro-football-hall-fame-class-2023-finalists-announced |website=ESPN.com |language=en |date=January 5, 2023}}</ref>

'''Alan Michael Reuber''' (born January 26, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M Aggies]]. He was signed by the [[Minnesota Vikings]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2004, but was released. He was then signed by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] and spent the season as a backup left tackle on the 53-man roster. Reuber was released the next season by Arizona, but would spend parts of the next two seasons on the Cardinals practice squad. Reuber was also a member of the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. He was also in camp with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in 2008.

'''Alan David Risher''' (born May 6, 1961) is a former [[quarterback]] for the LSU Tigers and the [[United States Football League]] (USFL), where he played for the [[Arizona Wranglers]].  The USFL was a 12 team league in 1983, so although Risher was drafted 170th overall in the league's 1983 draft, he was actually the team's 15th round pick that year.<ref>{{cite web | title = Arizona Wranglers 1983 Draft | work = USFL Info | url = http://www.usfl.info/wranglers/1983draft.html | access-date = February 12, 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121105054450/http://www.usfl.info/wranglers/1983draft.html | archive-date = 2012-11-05 | url-status = dead }}</ref>  Risher was the starting quarterback for the Wranglers for most of the league's initial 1983 season.  He is known best for directing what is widely acknowledged as the greatest upset in USFL history.  He backed up [[Greg Landry]] on the 1984 Western Conference Champion Wranglers squad.

He would later play in the [[National Football League]] for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and the [[Green Bay Packers]]<ref>{{cite web | title = Packers.com – Alan Risher | work = Packers.com | url = http://www.packers.com/history/all_time_roster/player/risher_alan_1987/ | archive-url = https://archive.today/20070810202959/http://www.packers.com/history/all_time_roster/player/risher_alan_1987/ | url-status = dead | archive-date = August 10, 2007 | access-date = October 7, 2008 }}</ref> going 2-1 as a starting quarterback for the Packers during the strike.<ref>{{cite web | title = Alan Risher Statistics | work = Pro Football Reference | url = https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RishAl20.htm | access-date = February 12, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090318115740/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RishAl20.htm| archive-date= 18 March 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>  Risher played collegiate ball for [[Louisiana State University]] from 1979-[[1982 LSU Tigers football team|1982]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Alan Risher Statistics | work = Pro Football Reference | url = https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RishAl20.htm | access-date = October 7, 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081011203351/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RishAl20.htm| archive-date= 11 October 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> Alan, has a son, Chad Risher, who owns his own business in Charlotte, North Carolina.<ref>{{cite web|last=Risher |first=Chad |url=http://www.risherbc.com |title=Risher Business Consultants, Inc |access-date=22 January 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120902013837/http://www.risherbc.com/ |archive-date=2 September 2012 }}</ref>

==Professional career==

===United States Football League===

====1983====
The matchup between the Arizona Wranglers and [[George Allen (American football coach)|George Allen]]'s Chicago Blitz that occurred Saturday, March 12, 1983, is widely considered the greatest upset in league history.

The Wranglers opened their initial season with two rookies competing for the starting quarterback job.  Risher and fellow rookie quarterback Todd Krueger of Northern Michigan had both played poorly in the teams' 24-0 opening loss to the Oakland Invaders, combining for 140 total yards passing on 32 attempts.  Wrangler coach [[Doug Shively]] decided to go with Risher as the starter in week 2, vs. the league's preseason title favorite, the [[Chicago Blitz]]. NFL veteran head coach [[George Allen (American football coach)|George Allen]] had stocked his Blitz team with NFL vets and CFL all-stars. Most media experts saw the Blitz as "NFL caliber" and thought the team would dominate the league. Some even questioned whether the Blitz would lose a game after seeing the team destroy the [[Craig James (running back)|Craig James]]-led [[Washington Federals]] in week one, 28–7.

The Wranglers, on the flipside, were assumed to be the league's worst team.  For three quarters, the matchup between the Blitz and Wranglers played to expectations. With 11:23 left in the fourth quarter Blitz quarterback, longtime NFL vet [[Greg Landry]], hit TE Paul Ricker with a 15-yard TD pass to put the Blitz up 29–12. After the ensuing kickoff, Risher brought his team to life.  He drove his team 85 yards down the field hitting [[Florida State University|FSU]] Rookie WR [[Jackie Flowers]] on a 10-yard TD pass.  The team successfully went for two, when Riser connected with [[University of Arizona]] Rookie TE [[Mark Keel]], cutting the lead to 29–20.  The Wrangler defense stiffened up and stopped the Blitz on the next series, forcing a punt.

After a short punt, Risher started on the Blitz 45 yard line and quickly took the team in for another score, this one a 9-yard pass to [[BYU]] rookie WR [[Neil Balholm]].  The kick was good and with 2:48 left in the game, the score was 29-27 Chicago. The Wranglers' Defense came up with another stop and after another punt, Risher and the offense had the ball on the Arizona 42 with 1:06 to play. Risher guided the team into field goal range and with one second left Wranglers kicker Jim Asmus kicked through the game winner.

The Wranglers improbable 30-29 come from behind victory over Chicago is considered by most to be the biggest upset in league history and one of that league's most important moments.<ref>{{cite web | title = Arizona Wranglers | work = Our Sports Central | url = http://www.oursportscentral.com/usfl/wrangler.htm | access-date = February 12, 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090309232345/http://www.oursportscentral.com/usfl/wrangler.htm| archive-date= 9 March 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>   The outcome of the game gave viability to the other teams in the league early in the season and told football fans that there was nothing inevitable about any USFL game's outcome.

Fueled by their comeback win, the young Wranglers flourished.  Risher started the next 4 games and led the team to a 3–3 record putting the team in a 4-way tie for the Pacific Division lead. Risher struggled in week 7, giving way to Krueger after 2 Interceptions in an ugly 44–23 loss to the potent [[Johnnie Walton]]-led [[Boston Breakers (USFL)|Boston Breakers]]. Risher came back to start the following week, throwing three touchdowns and playing an error free game, leading the Wranglers back into a tie for first in the division with a 24–3 victory over their Division rivals, the [[Denver Gold]].

From here the season collapsed for Risher and his 4-4 Wranglers. They would finish with a USFL record 10 straight losses.<ref>{{cite web|title=Remember the Arizona Wranglers |work=Remember the USFL |url=http://www.remembertheusfl.8m.com/teams/arizona.html |access-date=February 12, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090306223231/http://www.remembertheusfl.8m.com/teams/arizona.html |archive-date=6 March 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Although, Riser, Keel, Balholm, and Flowers would all end the season among the league leaders,<ref name="1983 USFL Statistical Leaders">{{cite web | title = 1983 USFL Statistical Leaders | work = USFL Info | url = http://www.usfl.info/1983stats.html | access-date = February 12, 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081005030542/http://www.usfl.info/1983stats.html | archive-date = October 5, 2008 | url-status = dead }}</ref> the team was legitimately among the youngest and least talented in the league.  The defense and offense were both inconsistent.  As the rest of the league rounded into midseason form, the offense struggled and the Wrangler D had difficulties keeping the games within reach.  Talent and depth shortfalls, the "Arizona heat", the young team collectively hitting a "rookie wall", and bad coaching are listed as possible factors credited with the collapse of the 1983 Wranglers.

Risher was generally solid if unspectacular down the stretch though he struggles in the Wrangler's 20–14 loss to the Tampa Bay Bandits in week 11, throwing 4 Interceptions. In weeks 14–16, COuch Doug Shively repeatedly removed Risher from the game. Risher did not play in weeks 17 and 18.

In spite of the team's finish, Risher would finish the season as the league's 6th ranked quarterback in 1983.<ref name="1983 USFL Statistical Leaders" />

====1984====
After the season, the Wranglers were sold to Blitz owner Dr. Ted Diethrich.  Coach Shively was fired.  The teams traded rosters with the exception of Risher, who stayed in Arizona to serve as backup to Landry on the 1984 Western Conference Champion Arizona Wranglers.  Risher would throw 103 passes in 1984 in relief of Landry.

===National Football League===

Risher was a member of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 1985 before being cut in the 1986 NFL preseason.<ref>{{cite web|title=NFL'S COLD CUTS SHOW IT'S A CRUEL BUSINESS|url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/news/os-xpm-1986-08-27-0250090177-story.html|first=Jerry|last=Greene|website=orlandosentinel.com|date=August 27, 1986|access-date=September 6, 2021}}</ref> He then started for the Green Bay Packers strike team in 1987, posting a career rating of 80.0 in the NFL in leading the team to a 2–1 record.

'''Alcender O'Neal Jackson''' (born May 18, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[Green Bay Packers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Alcender Jackson Statistics | work = Pro Football Reference | url = https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JackAl21.htm | accessdate = January 2, 2023 | archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20090108210540/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JackAl21.htm| archivedate= 8 January 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>

==Early life==
Jackson attended [[Moss Point High School]], where he was a two-time Class 5A All-state selection at [[offensive tackle]]. As a senior, he helped his team achieve a 12-1 record, while receiving [[All-American]] honors from SuperPrep magazine and being named Mississippi player of the year by the [[Jackson Clarion-Ledger]].

He accepted a football scholarship from [[Louisiana State University]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://tulsaworld.com/archives/southeastern-conference-signees/article_cd2ee47f-d65f-524f-b860-fdd6b4ce6bd2.html | title=Southeastern Conference Signees | accessdate=May 4, 2023}}</ref> As a freshman, he appeared in 5 games as backup. As a sophomore, he started 11 games at [[left tackle]]. As a junior, he started 5 games at left guard and missed 4 games with a sprained knee. As a senior, he started all games at left guard.

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
Jackson was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] after the [[2000 NFL draft]]. In [[training camp]], he was used at left and [[Guard (American football)|right guard]]. After making the team as a rookie, he was declared inactive for the first ten games and appeared in 3 of the last 6 contests. The next year, he was declared inactive for all of the regular season games.

In [[2002 Rhein Fire season|2002]], he was allocated to the [[Rhein Fire (NFL Europe)|Rhein Fire]] of [[NFL Europe]]. He received All-league honors at guard, after contributing to the team reaching [[World Bowl X]] and helping [[Jamal Robertson]] finish third in the league with 792 rushing yards and 8 [[touchdown]]s. The Cowboys waived him on September 1, [[2002 NFL season|2002]].

===Green Bay Packers===
On October 2, [[2002 NFL season|2002]], he was signed to the [[Green Bay Packers]] [[practice squad]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-2002-10-03-0210030386-story.html | title=Transactions | accessdate=May 4, 2023}}</ref> He was released on October 9. He was signed to the active roster on December 4 after [[Chad Clifton]] was lost for the season with a severe [[human pelvis|pelvic]] injury. He was cut on December 23, after appearing in 2 games.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-2002-12-24-0212240038-story.html | title=Transactions | accessdate=May 4, 2023}}</ref>

Athletic director | statlabel1 = Games | statvalue1 = 12 | pfr = HallAl22 }} '''Alan Glenn Haller''' (born August 9, 1970) is an American college athletic administrator and former [[American football|football]] player. He was previously the [[athletic director]] at [[Michigan State University]], a position he held from September 2021 to May 2025. Haller's 2022 salary was $800,000.{{cite web | url=https://openpayrolls.com/alan-haller-127707380 | title=Alan Haller | Vice President-Exec MGT | MSU | 2022 }} Haller played professionally as a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], [[Cleveland Browns]] and [[Carolina Panthers]]. He was selected in the fifth round of the [[1992 NFL draft]] by the Steelers. He played his first three games in the NFL with the Steelers before he was released and signed with the Cleveland Browns, where he played another three games. He returned to the Steelers in 1993 and joined the expansion [[Carolina Panthers]] in 1995 before retiring after the 1995 season. In his professional career, Haller played only 12 games in three seasons, earning no starts and no statistics. Though he was a defensive back, Haller played mostly as a special teams player. After retiring from the NFL, Haller returned to Michigan State University and became a police officer with the Michigan State University Department of Police and Public Safety. He spent 13 years on the force, eventually working his way up to 1st Lieutenant of the Uniform Division. In 2006, Haller, along with athletic director [[Mark Hollis (athletic director)|Mark Hollis]], men's basketball coach [[Tom Izzo]], and former athletic director [[Ron Mason]], was a member of the selection team that brought head football coach [[Mark Dantonio]] to Michigan State. In June 2010, Haller was named associate athletics director for administration for the Michigan State athletic department. He was the human resource officer for the athletics department and the student-athlete ombudsman. ==College football career== Haller attended Michigan State after attending [[J. W. Sexton High School]] in [[Lansing, Michigan]]. While in high school, Haller rushed for 1,245 yards and 14 touchdowns as a senior. He earned a scholarship to Michigan State and was converted into a defensive back by Spartans head coach [[George Perles]]. He was a three-year starter at both corner and safety. In 1991, he won the Co-Captains award for leadership. Haller finished his college career with three interceptions.{{Cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/alan-haller-1.html|title=Alan Haller College Stats}} ==NFL career== Haller was drafted by the Pittsburgh Steelers in the fifth round of the [[1992 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=1992 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1992/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} Though he made the team, he mainly played special teams, and was placed on waivers on November 17, 1992. The Cleveland Browns claimed Haller off waivers and like in Pittsburgh, Haller played mostly special teams. Less than a month after joining the Browns, Haller was injured and placed on Injured Reserved. The Browns released Haller in 1993 and he spent all of 1994 out of pro football. He later signed with the expansion [[Carolina Panthers]], appearing in just two games. The Panthers released Haller in camp the following summer, essentially ending his NFL career. ==Career after football== On September 1, 2021, Haller was named the athletic director at Michigan State University.{{Cite web|last=Solari|first=Chris|title=Former football player Alan Haller named Michigan State's 20th athletic director|url=https://www.freep.com/story/sports/college/michigan-state/spartans/2021/09/01/michigan-state-athletic-director-alan-haller-spartans/5681149001/|access-date=2021-09-01|website=Detroit Free Press|language=en-US}} Haller was the 20th athletic director in the school's history at that time. He had just prior served as the assistant vice president and deputy athletic director for Michigan State athletics.{{Cite web|title=Alan Haller - Staff Directory|url=https://msuspartans.com/staff-directory/alan-haller/9|access-date=2021-09-01|website=Michigan State University Athletics|language=en}} Michigan State University announced in May 2025 that Alan Haller is no longer serving as vice president and director of intercollegiate athletics, effective May 11, 2025. Prior to his tenure in the MSU Athletic Department, Haller was a police officer with the Michigan State University Police Department for 13 years. ==Personal life== Haller graduated from Michigan State with a B.A. in criminal justice and after his rookie season, he spent time as an intern in the Cleveland district attorney's office. He has two sons, Devin and Blake, and a daughter Allison. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [https://msuspartans.com/staff-directory/alan-haller/9 Michigan State profile] * {{Footballstats |nfl=alan-haller |espn= |cbs= |yahoo= |si= |pfr=H/HallAl22 |rotoworld= }} {{Michigan State Spartans athletic director navbox}} {{Big Ten Conference athletic director navbox}} {{Steelers1992DraftPicks}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Haller, Alan}} [[Category:1970 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American football defensive backs]] [[Category:Carolina Panthers players]] [[Category:Cleveland Browns players]] [[Category:Pittsburgh Steelers players]] [[Category:Michigan State Spartans athletic directors]] [[Category:Michigan State Spartans football players]] [[Category:Players of American football from Lansing, Michigan]] [[Category:African-American college athletic directors in the United States]] [[Category:African-American police officers]] [[Category:Law enforcement officials from Michigan]]

'''Albert Jamal McClellan'''<ref>{{cite web | title=ESPN Profile | work= ESPN.com | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/_/id/13851 }}</ref> (born June 4, 1986) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Marshall Thundering Herd football|Marshall Thundering Herd]] from 2005 to 2009, and was signed by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] after the [[2010 NFL draft]].

==Early life== 
A native of [[Lakeland, Florida]], McClellan attended [[Kathleen High School (Lakeland, Florida)|Kathleen High School]], where he was rated as a two-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]''.<ref>[https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Albert-McClellan-31466 Albert McClellan-Rivals.com] Retrieved August 15, 2012.</ref>

==College career==
McClellan played college football for [[Marshall Thundering Herd|Marshall]]. While there he was a three-time All-Conference USA selection, as well as the C-USA Defensive Player of the Year in 2006. He [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirted]] in 2007 after suffering a torn [[anterior cruciate ligament]] in pre-season, an injury that sidelined him for the year.<ref>{{Citation |url=http://marshall.scout.com/2/666898.html |title=Albert McClellan To Have Surgery, Out For '07 |work=Herd Insider magazine |first=Woody |last=Woodrum |date=August 10, 2007 |access-date=May 20, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716021322/http://marshall.scout.com/2/666898.html |archive-date=July 16, 2011 |url-status=dead }}.</ref>

===Baltimore Ravens===
McClellan was signed by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] as an undrafted free agent after the [[2010 NFL draft]]. McClellan played as the fourth string middle linebacker (Behind [[Ray Lewis]], [[Jameel McClain]], and [[Dannell Ellerbe]]). He did not play at all in the 2010 season, but saw limited time the next year.
With an injury to [[Terrell Suggs]] and the departure of [[Jarret Johnson]] to free agency in 2012, McClellan had a chance to compete for a starting outside linebacker spot with [[Paul Kruger (American football)|Paul Kruger]], [[Courtney Upshaw]], and [[Sergio Kindle]]. Upshaw appeared to have the edge for most of training camp, but in the third preseason game, McClellan got the start. He would start 11 games during the season, and would record 49 tackles and a sack, both career highs. The Ravens did go on to win [[Super Bowl XLVII]] after they beat the [[San Francisco 49ers]] 34–31.

On March 9, 2014, McClellan signed a new two-year contract to remain with the Ravens.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wilson|first=Aaron|title=Ravens agree to two-year deal with linebacker Albert McClellan, sources say|url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-sources-ravens-agree-to-twoyear-deal-with-linebacker-albert-mcclellan-20140309,0,4880860.story|publisher=Baltimoresun.com|access-date=March 9, 2014|archive-date=March 10, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310034431/http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-sources-ravens-agree-to-twoyear-deal-with-linebacker-albert-mcclellan-20140309,0,4880860.story|url-status=dead}}</ref>

McClellan signed a three-year extension to remain with Baltimore on March 1, 2016.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ravens, Albert McClellan agree to terms on three-year deal|url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-ravens-are-resigning-albert-mcclellan-20160301-story.html|website=BaltimoreSun.com|date=March 1, 2016|access-date=August 25, 2018|archive-date=August 26, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180826005218/http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-ravens-are-resigning-albert-mcclellan-20160301-story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2017 during training camp, McClellan tore his ACL and was ruled out for the season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Albert McClellan Out For The Year With Torn ACL|url=http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Albert-McClellan-Out-for-the-Year-With-Torn-ACL/686d5cd4-ff0f-4e4f-a7a6-cc379a56aa40|author=Mink, Ryan|website=BaltimoreRavens.com|date=August 28, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180322101819/http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Albert-McClellan-Out-for-the-Year-With-Torn-ACL/686d5cd4-ff0f-4e4f-a7a6-cc379a56aa40|archive-date=March 22, 2018}}</ref> He was placed on injured reserve on September 1, 2017.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ravens Announce 24 Roster Moves, Have 13 More To Make|url=http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Ravens-Announce-24-Roster-Moves-Have-13-More-to-Make/914aba64-f454-47d9-932f-e409ccec1735|author=Mink, Ryan|website=BaltimoreRavens.com|date=September 1, 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180118220814/http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Ravens-Announce-24-Roster-Moves-Have-14-More-to-Make/914aba64-f454-47d9-932f-e409ccec1735|archive-date=January 18, 2018}}</ref>

On November 6, 2018, McClellan was signed by the [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Patriots Make a Series of Roster Moves|url=https://www.patriots.com/news/patriots-make-a-series-of-roster-moves|website=Patriots.com|date=November 6, 2018}}</ref> In Week 14, McClellan blocked two punts on Dolphins punter [[Matt Haack]].  In the divisional round of the playoffs against the Los Angeles Chargers, McClellan recovered a fumble off a muffed punt.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Price |first1=Chris |title=#StayCovered Defensive Play of the Game – Albert McClellan's fumble recovery |url=https://www.bostonsportsjournal.com/2019/01/13/staycovered-defensive-play-game-albert-mcclellans-fumble-recovery/ |access-date=January 14, 2019}}</ref> The Patriots went on to win [[Super Bowl LIII]] 13–3 against the [[Los Angeles Rams]] to give McClellan his second Super Bowl title.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shpigel |first=Ben |date=February 4, 2019 |title=Patriots Win in Lowest-Scoring Super Bowl Ever |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/02/03/sports/patriots-super-bowl.html |access-date=October 31, 2023 |website=The New York Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

Bello, Place LB Albert McClellan on Injured Reserve|url=https://www.newyorkjets.com/news/jets-sign-lb-b-j-bello-place-lb-albert-mcclellan-on-injured-reserve|website=NewYorkJets.com|date=October 30, 2019|access-date=October 30, 2019|archive-date=October 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030155226/https://www.newyorkjets.com/news/jets-sign-lb-b-j-bello-place-lb-albert-mcclellan-on-injured-reserve|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''Alec Ogletree''' (born September 25, 1991) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Bulldogs football|University of Georgia]] and was selected by the [[St. Louis Rams]] in the first round of the [[2013 NFL draft]]. He also played in the NFL for the [[New York Giants]], [[New York Jets]], and [[Chicago Bears]].

==Early life==
Ogletree and his twin brother Alexander "Zander" were born in [[Newnan, Georgia]]. He attended [[Newnan High School]], where he played high school football and basketball and ran track for the Newnan Cougars. Regarded as one of the best teams in Newnan.He was widely considered to be one of the top football prospects of the 2010 high school class. He was rated as the No. 22 recruit by [[Scout.com]],<ref>[http://recruiting.scout.com/a.z?s=73&p=9&c=4&pid=88&yr=2010 Scout.com 2010 Rankings]. Recruiting.scout.com. Retrieved on June 27, 2014.</ref> the No. 29 recruit in the [[ESPNU]] 150,<ref>[https://archive.today/20110808162124/http://espn.go.com/college-football/recruiting/top150prospects/_/class/2010 ESPNU 150 2010 Rankings]. Espn.go.com. Retrieved on June 27, 2014.</ref> and the No. 40 player by [[Rivals.com]].<ref>[https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-2369 Rivals.com 2010 Rankings]. Sports.yahoo.com. Retrieved on June 27, 2014.</ref>

In his sophomore season, Ogletree had six blocked punts and returned one for a touchdown.<ref name="HSStats">{{Cite web |title=High School Stats |url=http://www.georgiadogs.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ogletree_alec00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231031948/http://www.georgiadogs.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ogletree_alec00.html |archive-date=December 31, 2010 |access-date=November 27, 2010 |publisher=GeorgiaDogs.com}}</ref> He had 75 tackles, three interceptions and six blocked punts as a junior.<ref name="HSStats" /> In his senior year, Ogletree had 85 tackles, 5 tackles for loss, 2 forced fumbles, two interceptions and two blocked kicks on defense—and he had 33 receptions for 633 yards and 5 touchdowns on offense.<ref name="HSStats" />

Also a standout [[track and field]] athlete, Ogletree was one of the state's top performers in the long jump. He captured the state title in the [[long jump]] event at the 2010 GHSA Region 4-AAAAA track and field championships, with a PR leap of 7.30 [[meters]] (23 ft, 11 in).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Region 4-AAAAA (Girls and Boys) 2010 - Complete Results (Raw) |url=https://ga.milesplit.com/meets/70178-region-4-aaaaa-girls-and-boys-2010/results/120170/raw |access-date=2024-01-10 |website=MileSplit GA |language=en}}</ref> He also ran the 400-meter dash and was a member of the Newnan 4×100-meter relay squad.

Following his senior season in 2009, he was recognized as a high school All-American by [[Under Armour]], ''[[USA Today]]'', and ''[[Parade magazine|Parade]]''. Ogletree verbally committed to attend the University of Georgia in June 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MKRob Media |url=http://www.mkrob.com/newnan-hs-ga-s-ogletree-commits-to-georgia/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714104423/http://www.mkrob.com/newnan-hs-ga-s-ogletree-commits-to-georgia/ |archive-date=July 14, 2011 |access-date=November 28, 2010 |website=www.mkrob.com}}</ref> He made his commitment official by signing his [[letter of intent]] to play at Georgia on February 3, 2010,<ref>[http://www.times-herald.com/Local/Ogletrees--others-sign-letters-of-intent-74857 Ogletrees, others sign letters of intent; UGA, Georgia Tech signee lists] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717060740/http://www.times-herald.com/Local/Ogletrees--others-sign-letters-of-intent-74857 |date=July 17, 2011 }}. Times-herald.com (February 10, 2010). Retrieved on June 27, 2014.</ref> choosing it over tens of other Division-1 schools including the [[University of Alabama]], [[Auburn University]], [[University of Florida]], and [[Florida State University]].<ref>[https://sports.yahoo.com/footballrecruiting/football/recruiting/player-Alec-Ogletree-84162/ Rivals.com Profile of Alec Ogletree]. Sports.yahoo.com. August 17, 2009.</ref> His brother Zander also went to UGA, playing fullback.

==College career==
Ogletree received an athletic scholarship to attend the [[University of Georgia]], where he played for coach [[Mark Richt]]'s [[Georgia Bulldogs football]] team from 2010 to 2012.

In 2010, Ogletree returned from his one-game suspension and was inserted into all the special team units.<ref name="FreshmanYear">{{Cite web |last=Page |first=Fletcher |date=November 12, 2010 |title=Ogletree grows into starting role |url=http://www.macon.com/2010/11/12/1337733/ogletree-grows-into-starting-role.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101115021229/http://www.macon.com/2010/11/12/1337733/ogletree-grows-into-starting-role.html |archive-date=November 15, 2010 |access-date=November 27, 2010 |publisher=Macon.com |df=mdy-all}}</ref> He eventually started getting some small amounts of playing time at safety. He was inserted into the starting strong safety spot for the final 3 games of the regular season for Georgia.

In 2011, Ogletree broke his foot during the first quarter of Georgia's season opener vs. [[2011 Boise State Broncos football team|Boise State]].<ref name="BrokenFoot">{{Cite web |last=Low |first=Chris |date=September 4, 2011 |title=Alec Ogletree out 4–6 weeks |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/6931550/alec-ogletree-georgia-bulldogs-broken-foot-4-6-weeks |access-date=September 8, 2011 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> He missed the following six games, returning for the [[2011 Florida Gators football team|Florida]] game on October 29. Against No. 1 LSU in the [[2011 SEC Championship Game]], he recorded 6 tackles including two for a loss, 1 sack and recovered a 1st quarter onside kick. In a little over 8 games, Ogletree finished the 2011 season with 52 tackles (6.5 per game) including 7.5 for a loss, 3 sacks, 2 forced fumbles and a pass deflection that was intercepted.

===St. Louis / Los Angeles Rams===
====2013====
The [[St. Louis Rams]] selected Ogletree in the first round (30th overall) of the [[2013 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2013 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2013/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-14 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Ogletree was the second linebacker drafted in 2013, behind [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia's]] [[Jarvis Jones]] (17th overall, Steelers).<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 25, 2013 |title=Rams Select Alec Ogletree With the 30th pick in 1st Round |work=therams.com |url=http://www.therams.com/news-and-events/article-1/Rams-Select-Alec-Ogletree-With-the-30th-pick-in-1st-Round/45b01eaf-99b3-407c-a13a-133b35cd58d6 |url-status=dead |access-date=March 7, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170518130140/http://www.therams.com/news-and-events/article-1/Rams-Select-Alec-Ogletree-With-the-30th-pick-in-1st-Round/45b01eaf-99b3-407c-a13a-133b35cd58d6 |archive-date=May 18, 2017}}</ref> On July 14, 2013, the Rams signed Ogletree to a four-year, $7.03 million contract that includes $5.66 million guaranteed and a [[signing bonus]] of $3.49 million.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Overthecap.com: Alec Ogletree contract |url=https://overthecap.com/player/alec-ogletree/2211 |access-date=July 6, 2018 |website=Overthecap.com}}</ref><ref name="spotrac">{{Cite web |title=Spotrac.com: Alec Ogletree contract |url=https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/new-york-giants/alec-ogletree-12310/ |access-date=July 6, 2018 |website=Spotrac.com}}</ref>
